title: Why Ocon isn't receiving the new Haas power unit in Monza
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix is a big weekend for Haas as the team brings its first major upgrade package since Canada back in May.

The VF-26 has slipped towards the tail of the midfield pack in recent races, having been jumped by Aston Martin’s AMR26. There’s also been a rollercoaster of form between Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon, with typically one struggling and the other a lot happier on a given weekend.

For Monza there’s also an extra boost for Bearman, who gets the sole example of the latest Ferrari power unit – upgraded through the ADUO process – that has been allocated to customer team Haas.

“We are very much hoping that we have a bit more performance this weekend,” Bearman said on Thursday. “It’s been a good few races now that we’ve kind of been left behind by our competition. It’s been a while that we’ve brought a big upgrade to the car, and so we have a lot of hopes set on this one.

“It seems like a big one, and all of the team are quite confident. Monza, it’s maybe not the best place to bring upgrades necessarily, because you don’t see the full effect of the benefit, of course, with this track, which is a much more drag-sensitive one than maybe last week was.

“Nonetheless, it’s been a long time coming. The team have worked incredibly hard, and we have a lot of challenges that we face. Being a small team, one of them is the turnaround times of our upgrades, and you’ve seen that. The last big one that we brought was in Canada, which is a long way back. Hopefully it’s going to be a good weekend for us.”

Ocon, who had a few difficult races in the middle of the season, is equally upbeat about the upgrades.

“I'm excited to drive this new car,” said the Frenchman. “Obviously, we have the new aero package. I drove it in the simulator on Tuesday, and yeah, it felt better there. Of course, we need to translate it to the track. It's not always a given that it will perform like that on track.

“But everybody's excited in the office, and looking forward to see what this car can do. And obviously, it's not the most technical circuit for it, so we are not going to see the full gain. We are more going to see that in Madrid. But it will still be interesting to see how the car feels in the Lesmos and Parabolica compared to before. So it is quite a big package, and I'm looking forward to driving it.”

Ocon’s suggestion that it’s a “new car” gives some idea of the scale of the upgrade package, and that’s backed up by the strategy that the team has adopted for the weekend.

In the past it has often conducted back-to-back tests between new and old spec cars on Friday, and then converted the latter for Saturday.

This time both cars are in the new spec from the start of FP1, a reflection of the fact that changing on Friday evening would be a huge job – and likely involve playing a curfew joker.

“Ideally, we want to back-to-back it,” said Team Principal Ayao Komatsu. “But because of the parts involved, it's very difficult to back-to-back, like to combat the car on Friday night, for instance, that was going to be challenging. One to break the curfew, two, in terms of quality of the job we can do.

“Yes, it's nice to actually measure exactly how much performance you put on the car, but at the same time we don't want to risk that Friday night s**t fight. But also, let's face it, if we had a car capable of scoring points at the baseline, we might take a different view.

“But if we don't do anything, we're not going to score points. So we rather put it all in, believe that it's going to work, and then make sure that we do a very good quality preparation.”

As mentioned earlier only Bearman has the new Ferrari power unit this weekend, and why he and not Ocon has the benefit of it is an interesting tale in itself, given that usually Haas try to be as fair as possible across the two cars.

Ferrari is only obliged to provide its customer teams with one upgraded power unit when the works cars get a new spec. In essence given the need to squeeze out everything possible at Monza, Haas did not want to wait until two were available just to be fair to both drivers. Thus the difficult choice was made to give only one car the benefit.

“Last time around we didn't do that,” Komatsu confirmed. “We waited until we had enough engines to introduce to both drivers together. Obviously Monza, as you know, it's a very power-sensitive circuit. So it's a shame to have performance sitting in the garage, right?

“Of course, it makes it very challenging. So yes, it would have been better if two engines are available at least. But again, Ferrari is pushing like hell to get as much performance on the engine as possible. Of course, they want to introduce it at Monza, for the reasons I just said to you. So that means they’ve got minimum quantity, just to satisfy the regulation.”

So why did Bearman get the nod? He’s ahead of Ocon in the World Championship, but that wasn’t the only factor at play.

“Of course, that's part of the consideration,” said Komatsu. “But again, it's not an aerodynamic upgrade, but the last items we had, like the CI [Carbon Industrie] brakes test, Esteban was actually struggling more on brake locking, etcetera. So considering that the Montreal upgrade, we got it on Ollie first, we decided to give that brake upgrade to Esteban first.

“We had another upgrade on the power steering before shutdown in Budapest. Again, we decided to give that to Esteban, because again he was more vocal about it, and he was struggling more on the power steering feel. So the last two upgrades we gave to Esteban – this this time around it's a back to Ollie.”

title: Why Tsunoda feels ‘like a rookie’ for Racing Bulls return
excerpt:
When Yuki Tsunoda was told he would be driving for Racing Bulls at the Dutch Grand Prix, he was on holiday on a beach in Greece and had to rush to prepare for the outing at Zandvoort. He felt so unprepared that he approached the weekend like a rookie.

By the time the Italian Grand Prix came around, Tsunoda had already been working in the simulator in case Isack Hadjar remained sidelined. Despite having a race weekend in the car under his belt and more time to prepare, he still feels like a rookie given the complexity of energy deployment at Monza.

“It was actually yesterday,” Tsunoda said on Thursday when asked when he had learned the news. “I was in the sim just in case. I really didn't know until mid-afternoon, and I heard in the middle of the session. ‘OK, I’m going to drive, so I’ll keep doing the simulator work as I would in a race week.’”

Zandvoort went about as well as could have been expected, given Tsunoda’s unfamiliarity with the car and the demands of a Sprint weekend. After finishing a solid P11, he received positive feedback from Team Principal Alan Permane.

“[It was] positive for sure,” the Japanese racer confirmed. “And even after the debrief, I said, ‘Good luck this season, I enjoyed it,’ or something. Alan said, ‘We might need you again – we might need you again next week. So be prepared.’

“I could tell that I felt some more trust from him after that race. If I did really bad, and anything can happen with this world, maybe I wouldn't get called to drive this week. So yeah, I think this was very positive.”

Although final confirmation came late, Tsunoda had spent the days after Zandvoort assuming he might be needed. He therefore focused on training, working with the Faenza engineers and running in the simulator.

“I was pretty much really chilled, like a usual race week. I was more prepared, I would say, than the week before in the Netherlands, because it all happened suddenly, and now after Isack was injured, I was more prepared.

Lawson to replace Hadjar again at Red Bull in Monza

“So that was probably the healthiest one week I spent in 2026 so far! So yeah, I was really prepared. I'm feeling more ready than ever.”

The biggest challenge now is energy deployment around Monza, an area where Tsunoda lacks the race experience of the drivers who have competed throughout this season, taking in the long straights at places like Shanghai and Spa-Francorchamps.

“I think Netherlands was fortunately one of the easiest tracks I would say to manage the energy, and I can say that I was able to adjust to the car pretty smoothly," said Tsunoda.

“But now it's the most difficult track for that energy deployment, and I already experienced in the simulator how different it is, and really kicks in these challenges of these regulations.

“So yeah, the management, brake early or whatever, those things I really have to practice. And in the simulator, it felt really weird, because I know I can drive faster – but you cannot, because otherwise in total lap time, you'll be slow. So that will be the biggest challenge for me.”

Being quick over a single lap is one thing, but Tsunoda must also adjust to the tactical, energy-management battles that were less prominent at Zandvoort.

“I think it will be more challenging in race condition,” he admitted. “Because this kind of strategic, I would say, battle with the energy management with other cars, I didn't do that, and probably other [drivers] know what the car is going to do after they use the battery to overtake or defend. I only know from the simulator, and the Netherlands was probably the least powerful.

“In short runs I would say I'm not worried as much, because you have free practice anyway, so you know what kind of things, and you can only focus on yourself. But in the race, you have to be proactive, right? So that's the only thing that I have to be more prepared for sure than the Netherlands.”

Tsunoda is hoping to take a step forward from Zandvoort, with a place in Q3 and points on Sunday his ideal scenario. However, he knows it will not be easy.

"I will see for FP1 these energy things, how difficult it is. I really don't know. But I think the car pace is good, and we’re bringing an upgrade here, so I am excited to see that.

“I think the Netherlands was more like I just entered the race a bit like a rookie, so I just tried to learn as much as possible. The time was very tight because of the Sprint format.

“I have to practice a lot of things, like energy deployments, and even over one lap to be patient. I would say I feel like I'm a rookie, and I have to try and learn everything, and try to not miss any single thing that the team is instructing me.”

He also has a special reason to want a good result this weekend: “I want to do well here – I’ve never done well here. Out of five years, I have three DNFs, two I didn't even start. So I don't know what's going on with here, but getting this opportunity, hopefully it’s lucky.”

title: Verstappen sets out target for Monza
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has admitted that he and Red Bull “need to be realistic” about their chances at the upcoming Italian Grand Prix, with the Dutchman setting out the aim of “just trying to have a good weekend”.

Verstappen’s home event last time out in Zandvoort ended in disappointing fashion after he suffered a crash at the end of the first lap, putting him out of the running while stand-in team mate Liam Lawson salvaged points for the squad in P7.

Looking ahead to Monza, Verstappen will sit out Free Practice 1 as Ayumu Iwasa gets behind the wheel before he returns to action for FP2 – and while it is a track that he claimed victory at last season, the four-time World Champion is keeping his expectations modest this time around.

“Let's see,” he said of his prospects. “Of course I'm not doing FP1, so we'll see afterwards how the car will be. Trying to get it into a nice window, but at the same time we also need to be realistic, where we are at the moment as a team and how we're performing.

“We’ll just try to have a good weekend. I know it's already going to be very complex with the energy around here, so we just need to try and understand that first and then we'll just see from there where we are in the pecking order.

“Just going off the last few races, I think we just need to be realistic.”

Looking back at the difficult end to what will be the last Dutch Grand Prix, Verstappen conceded that he does not think it would have been a particularly strong outing even if he had been able to continue.

“I would have loved to have completed the race, even though I don’t think it would have been a magic race for us pace-wise,” he explained.

“The whole weekend we were a bit off, and I was not feeling well so all the combinations were not there.

“But I look back at it with a lot of positives – I won races there, we had really great moments with the fans there, so overall it was a crazy experience and I’m very happy that I got to have a home Grand Prix like that.”

title: Why Piastri wants answers to a ‘bigger question’ in Monza
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri believes he and McLaren have "got ideas on how we can make things better" ahead of this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, after the Australian has struggled for performance in recent races.

Team mate and reigning World Champion Lando Norris has put McLaren back on top in Formula 1 after winning the two previous races in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Although Piastri fought for the win in the former before retiring, he was noticeably lacking pace compared with Norris at Zandvoort, finishing 32 seconds adrift of the race winner.

The Dutch Grand Prix marked a complete year since Piastri stood on the top step of the podium, having watched his lead in last year's drivers' standings eventually surpassed by Norris.

Speaking on Thursday's media day ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, Piastri admitted that his struggles were not due to one reason specifically, making it harder to rectify.

"I think it's never been the same issue or thing we're chasing every weekend. It's always been slightly different which I think kind of raises a bigger question," he said.

"If it was just one thing we kept struggling with it would, in some ways, be a bit of an easy fix but I think the fact we've kind of found different ways of having difficulty, we've been trying to answer that question.

"And we are getting closer, finding more ideas and ultimately the only way you can really solve it is by trying stuff on track. Not saying that we've gone away and found this problem, we've definitely got ideas on how we can make things better, both from how I drive the car and how we set up the car.

"Hopefully we can find something that works a bit better. I think in Zandvoort, Qualifying was a much bigger step, Lando and I were very close but clearly in the race there was a deficit. That's the area we're trying to work on."

Piastri believes that the new-for-2026 regulations have created a breed of car which he has struggled to adapt to, while bad luck and reliability problems have also played their part.

"There's definitely things that have not been as easy or as comfortable this year compared to last year," he said.

"Some things we can fix quickly, some things we can't. I think these cars in general, the concept is very different, the tyres are quite different.

"There's a lot of things as well that are not necessarily in our control. Also this season not been easy for other reasons, we've had a lot of struggles with reliability or bad luck."

title: Russell reveals Mercedes’ Monza Qualifying plan
excerpt:
George Russell has revealed that Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli is primed to help him with a tow during Qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix, despite their respective quests for the 2026 world title.

Russell arrives at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza 59 points behind Antonelli in the Drivers’ Championship standings, having claimed two Grand Prix victories to the Italian’s six so far this season.

Antonelli, however, will drop to the back of the grid for his home race due to a full power unit change, ruling him out of pole position contention before the weekend has even started.

That has raised questions over whether Antonelli might be used to support Russell’s own bid for pole by providing a slipstream along one of Monza’s many long straights – in turn giving the Briton a valuable top-speed boost.

Giving his response during Thursday’s media duties, Russell initially smiled, “I hope so”, before explaining that “they offered it” and “we’ll go for it, see if it works” as Qualifying develops.

He continued: “It’s not maybe as powerful as it once was with the wings open in [Straight Mode] the whole time, but we’ll work as a team. That’s how we do things.”

In terms of Antonelli’s impending grid drop having any other impact on his preparations and approach to the weekend, Russell’s take was clear.

“For me, it doesn’t change anything, because I always want to focus on myself, focus on my limitations and the areas I want to improve,” he said.

“I always said it doesn’t matter if I have a seven-time World Champion as my team mate or a rookie. The job is still the same, so my approach will be exactly the same.”

He added: “I think I’m feeling much better since the summer break, and hoping just to continue building on that momentum.

“Of course, we know we’ve got fierce competition at the moment with McLaren and Ferrari bringing upgrades. We’re still on the back foot in terms of bringing these upgrades to the car.

“We know in that interim it’s not going to be as straightforward as it once was, but hoping to fight for pole and the win again.”

Nonetheless, Russell suggested that “any of the top-four teams” have the potential to succeed this weekend – again being quick to highlight McLaren after their back-to-back victories in Hungary and the Netherlands.

“We can say all we want [about the pecking order], but we’ll soon find out,” he commented. “I think there will be a lot of tough competition.

“The momentum is with McLaren right now. Ferrari has upgrades this weekend. We know Red Bull has a strong power unit. So, I honestly think this weekend it could be between any of the top-four teams, but I hope it’s us.”

title: Norris evaluates chances of victory hat-trick in Monza
excerpt:
Lando Norris is optimistic that he can continue his superb form and win the Italian Grand Prix, but was keen to emphasise that McLaren still have plenty to work on when it comes to their place in the pecking order.

After a lacklustre start to the 2026 season, the reigning World Champion finally returned to the top step at the Hungarian Grand Prix, following the achievement with another hard-fought win in the Netherlands to make him the only non-Mercedes driver to claim back-to-back victories so far.

Although Norris has a chance to extend that streak in Monza, he admitted that predicting a result would be a pointless exercise due to how differently the car behaves at each circuit.

Asked how confident he felt about completing the hat-trick of wins, he said: “It's certainly the plan. It's still hard to know, I think we're at the stage where it's hard to predict where we're going to be.

“I think we also don't want to waste time trying to predict these things. We're just focused, working on the stuff that's in our control. I'm doing the same. Clearly in a good place as a whole team at the minute, we know we have things we really have to try and work on and improve and we'll see if we've been able to make any progress into this weekend.

“Looking forward to it, it's another weekend where we want to be hopeful and believe it's possible. We kind of just have to wait and see.

“It's another track where we want to prove things. I wouldn't say it's a bad circuit for us, we've been good here in the past. I think there are still tracks ahead that I'm not looking forward to quite as much. There's still some good high-speed corners here which we want to try and make use of.

“Still a very long season, lots of different types of tracks we still have ahead of us. The goal is to continue the performances we've had lately, but we'll have to see tomorrow how the pace is and see if we can have another good weekend.”

Norris will be further buoyed by his latest contract that will see him remain at McLaren until the end of 2030, becoming the second driver on the grid to commit to a significant long-term deal after Max Verstappen made a similar announcement ahead of his home race.

“I just love where I am, simple as that,” Norris said of the news. “I don't want to change, don't want to be with other people. Don't want to have a reset and work with anyone else. Happy that I'm with people I love to spend time with, create memories.

“They're my family, [the] team I've been with since beginning in F1, and they're also the team that I believe can help me win races and win more championships. For me there's two big reasons, the people and the performance that we have.

“Not everything in life is about performance, I just want to be places that I'm happy and for now, only been with one team and I'm happy with them.”

title: Colapinto grateful for Alpine ‘trust’ amid contract extension
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto has praised the “trust” from Alpine after agreeing a contract extension with the team, ahead of a weekend in which the Argentinian is hoping an upgrade package can give the Enstone-based outfit an advantage over their rivals.

Another piece of the 2027 driver market fell into place when it was recently confirmed that Colapinto will continue to race for the squad next season, forming an unchanged line-up alongside Pierre Gasly.

It comes after a solid start to the campaign for Colapinto, who has scored 19 points and sits in P12 of the Drivers’ Championship.

“I’m very pleased, very happy,” the 23-year-old said of the news during Thursday’s media day at the Italian Grand Prix. “I’m very excited for what's coming and to continue this journey with the team.

“I'm very grateful for the opportunities this last year, and we grew up a lot together, a big family now. We did a lot of steps together as a team, improving the car in many areas, improving the performance of everyone in the team. I’m happy and looking forward to keep it going.”

Colapinto went on to express his gratitude for the opportunity that he was handed by Executive Advisor Flavio Briatore and “the trust since the start”, adding that he is “very happy with the effort of the team, how we improved lately and the steps that we’ve made together as a family”.

The announcement comes as the driver from Buenos Aires prepares to race with an upgrade package in Monza, with the new parts set to go on both Alpine cars after Gasly ran with them last time out in Zandvoort.

“I think Monza is always a track I enjoy driving, aside of having the upgrade or not,” said Colapinto. “With it, I think it's going to be good. Hopefully it's a good track for us – we'll see how it looks on Friday.

“It’s going to be important to keep working and trying to extra everything out of the car in Qualifying.”

Scoring points in the Netherlands has helped Alpine to move closer to Racing Bulls in the battle for P5 of the Teams’ Championship, with the gap now standing at just three points.

“We are really close,” Colapinto conceded. “With the last upgrade we did a very good step in terms of performance and we are closer to them, which was our goal. We were hoping to do a big step and it happened, and the upgrade is working well, but we need to keep working and putting everything together to be in front of them.

“They are fast, Audi is fast as well. They are bringing I think an upgrade here with the rear wing, so they will be a bit faster, but we have trust in the package we have now and hopefully we can extract everything and be in front.”

title: Leclerc targets ‘very special’ Monza weekend with new engine
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has echoed team mate Lewis Hamilton’s optimism over an engine upgrade that Ferrari will deploy at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza – expressing his hope of delivering another “very special weekend” in front of the Tifosi.

After an initial update in Austria earlier this season, Ferrari have made further changes to their power unit for the Italian Grand Prix, as part of the team’s 2026 ‘ADUO’ (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) allowance.

With Hamilton talking about the possibility of challenging for victory on Ferrari’s home soil earlier in the day, Leclerc shared similar ambitions when he faced the media – as he pushes to claim what would be third win in red at the famous Temple of Speed.

Asked about the engine update, and what he expects it to bring, Leclerc replied: “It will have a bit more power, which is always a good thing. How much more power? Only time will tell.

“I’ll do my best in order to have a very special weekend like in 2019 and 2024, which are probably the best memories I have in racing, together with [the win in] Monaco in 2024.

“But we are against very tough competition and the engine is definitely our weak part. To do a step forward will help us close a little bit the gap to the guys in front.”

However, Leclerc went on to highlight the “perfect execution” that will be required if Ferrari are to triumph for the third time this season – after Hamilton’s win in Barcelona and the Monegasque’s win at Silverstone.

“If there’s one track we can afford to maybe compromise a little bit Qualifying compared to the race, it’s this one,” he said. “However, our job is to make the car faster, and that will be beneficial for Qualifying and the race.

“On a track like this, we expect to have a bit of a harder time because it’s lots of straight lines and we know that this is a bit of a weak point compared to our competitors so far, but I’m still optimistic.

“Silverstone and Spa weren’t meant to be positive for us and we had a good weekend, but by having a perfect execution. We need to target that here.

“We have a new engine, we have new parts on the car, and I hope that helps us to put the others under a bit more pressure.”

As for how much energy he takes from racing in Ferrari’s backyard, Leclerc added: “Italy has always been very special for me. I kind of grew up here through my karting career, I was very much living with my mechanics here, and so I have a very special connection with Italy and the people.

“To be racing with Ferrari in Italy is already a special experience, but even more so for me. I just really hope we can convert all that positive excitement into a victory on Sunday.”

title: Lawson details ‘biggest challenge’ of Red Bull switch
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained how having to carry out Italian Grand Prix preparation with both Red Bull and Racing Bulls has proven to be the “biggest challenge” of switching seats, with the news that he would again drive for the former not coming until Wednesday.

Lawson stepped in at the Milton Keynes-based squad last time out in Zandvoort after Isack Hadjar suffered a wrist injury prior to the event, the New Zealander going on to score points with a P7 finish in Sunday’s race.

It was then announced just before the paddock headed to Monza that Hadjar would again sit out the weekend as his rehabilitation continues, meaning that Lawson will drive alongside Max Verstappen at the team for another outing while Yuki Tsunoda gets a second opportunity in Lawson’s place at Racing Bulls.

Asked during Thursday’s media day about when he learned he would be racing for Red Bull again, Lawson responded: “Wednesday. So, for the last week, it's been sort of just waiting to see. Obviously, trying to give Isack the best chance as well for his recovery.

“But, yeah, I think in the back of my mind, I knew that obviously there was still a chance. Obviously, only being on Wednesday, it felt quite late, but we had enough time to still do a simulator session and normal prep for the weekend.”

Quizzed further on which team’s engineers he had been talking with as he carried out his preparation for the weekend, the 24-year-old said: “Both, honestly. I’ve been doing both, just to try and stay ready for both. Obviously, both teams, both cars to know.

“They're very different to drive, so it's not the easiest thing going between the two, even just in the simulator, but that's been the biggest challenge. But it's nice to finally have an answer, from Wednesday, to know that I can basically just put all my focus onto this car.”

Lawson went on to explain that the Red Bull and Racing Bulls cars are different “everywhere”, adding: “Other than the power unit, obviously, they're very different to drive.

“The main thing with the Red Bull, the high-speed grip is probably the most impressive just coming from my car. But the way they drive, the balance of the car is very, very different.

“So, yeah, without saying too much, it is a very different car to drive. Honestly, the feedback I get through the steering, everything, the way it feels, the way it moves around, it's very different.”

Despite the challenge of adapting between the two, Lawson is keen to maximise the opportunity of driving the RB22 again during the weekend ahead at Monza.

“[My mindset is to] just try and make the most of it,” he explained. “Again, I think it's an interesting position for me to be in. Zandvoort was, being a Sprint weekend, obviously quite stressful at times, but overall it was a good weekend.

“And at least now I've had that, it should be a bit easier to adjust. We also have three practice sessions here. It's a much more normal weekend, so, yeah, it's another good opportunity.”

title: Kimi Antonelli issues hilarious 'shut up' response: 'Don't joke with me'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli issued a hilarious response ahead of this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix, with his comments harking back to his dramatic Formula 1 debut at Monza two years ago.

The 20-year-old made his debut in first practice at Monza for Mercedes in 2024 and immediately looked quick. However, he exceeded the limits too quickly and crashed early on at Parabolica.

It was a saddening end to his debut and was something that he has since conceded played on his mind at last year’s Italian GP.

This time around, though, Antonelli is in a very different mindset and at a very different confidence level, in what has been an extraordinary 2026.

He enters the weekend in Italy with a 59-point lead in the drivers’ standings and six victories to his name. A seventh win at Monza is unlikely, as he will start from the back due to a grid penalty triggered by a full engine change.

It has been a rollercoaster two years for the young Italian, who would not have believed, had he been told after his crash, that he would find himself leading the standings today.

Asked what he would have said if someone told him at Monza two years ago after crashing that he would be leading the title entering the 2026 Italian GP, Antonelli told select media, including RacingNews365: "I would say to shut up. Yeah. Just don't joke with me.

"I mean, of course, it was a very difficult day for me, very difficult moment because definitely that was not the way I wanted to introduce myself into the sport. And, definitely, crashing out so early on... Yes, I was pushing. It was going well, but it lasted very short.

"But it was not the way I wanted to start everything. So it was a very difficult moment and a very difficult period as well, the one following, because it's not easy to get over these kind of things, especially at the very beginning.

"So, of course, if someone, while I was walking off in the gravel, would have said, 'What, in two years they're going to be leading the world championship in this exact moment,' I would have said, 'Probably you're just kidding.'

"But, you know, it's happening. And, I'm very, very, very happy, very grateful. And, yeah, just got to keep pushing.:

title: Colton Herta suffers huge accident just before latest Cadillac F1 outing
excerpt:
The American driver will be participating in F1 Free Practice 1 at the Italian Grand Prix for Cadillac.

Colton Herta suffered a huge accident in FIA F2 practice at Monza, in the worst possible preparation ahead of his latest F1 outing for Cadillac.

Herta is due to take over Sergio Perez's MAC-26 in F1 Free Practice 1 later in the morning at Monza for his third FP1 outing of the season.

However, with around 15 minutes remaining in the sole F2 practice session, the American dipped his left-side wheels into the gravel rounding the second Lesmo corner.

The Hitech driver then span across the track and into the barrier on the other side of the circuit, with the rear of the car being destroyed as it lay stricken in the middle of the circuit.

Herta climbed out uninjured from the car and was transported back to the paddock for a debrief with his engineers and to prepare to take over Perez's car in F1 practice.

title: McLaren finally unleash 'H-wing' as Mercedes title pursuit hots up
excerpt:
The upgrades list for the 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix is in, and McLaren are preparing to unleash a key upgrade.

McLaren will finally unleash its version of the 'Macarena' F1 rear wing at the Italian Grand Prix, with the system being dubbed the 'H-wing.'

Ferrari pioneered the system in pre-season testing, with Red Bull following soon after, but McLaren's version has been delayed and was run on-track for the first time in FP1 in Hungary, but not in qualifying or the race.

For Monza, with its straight-line speed demands, the draggy MCL40 machine is to be fitted with the 'H-wing', so-called for the 'H' in sponsor Etihad on the rear wing, akin to the F-duct of 2010 which covered the 'F' in Vodafone, a then sponsor.

McLaren has also brought "updated floor furniture" to better direct the airflow and improve aerodynamic performance, whilst also trying to shed more drag.

Elsewhere, Red Bull has some upgrades to the RB22, with a revised floor body aiming to increase local load and aerodynamic stability, with an exhaust tailpipe also being delivered to suit the demands of Monza. A new front wing with tweaked end-plate vanes will also be evaluated.

Mercedes has not brought any performance upgrades, instead only bringing its low-downforce specification of wings and bodywork, as has Ferrari, whose major work has been done under the engine cover with a new ADUO-upgraded engine.

The article continues below.

Elsewhere, Williams has also shipped its low-downforce spec to Monza with no performance upgrades, with Racing Bulls having followed suit, but does have a new exhaust tailpipe aiming to "improve the flow management around the centreline of the car" to boost performance.

Aston Martin has brought a new front suspension with revised fairings and a new floor edge for Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll, with Haas also bringing a big upgrade as it seeks to recover lost momentum.

A new floor, bodywork and rear corner will be delivered for Oliver Bearman and Esteban Ocon, with the general idea being to improve airflow management and increase downforce.

Alpine has a new front-wing endplate to increase local load and a rear wing tweak with the SM pod fairing removed to boost straight-line speed.

Cadillac has a new floor and diffuser sidewall vane to increase load at the rear of the car.

Audi has submitted no upgrades for the weekend.

title: Revealed: How Ferrari has fixed a key problem with second ADUO engine upgrade
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix this weekend at Monza holds special significance for Ferrari. Not because it is their home race, but because it could effectively serve as a crucial turning point for assessing just how realistic their chances are of challenging Mercedes for both world titles from now until the end of the season.

This is because, as is well known, Ferrari will introduce an upgraded power unit on the SF-26, based on the development opportunities granted by the FIA through the allocation of the second ADUO of the season. These modifications can only affect the internal combustion engine, since the FIA has adopted a metric that evaluates the performance deficit based solely on the internal combustion engine’s performance, without considering the overall performance, which also includes the electric component.

The power unit developed by the team led by Enrico Gualtieri had followed a very specific design path, based in part on the use of a smaller-diameter turbo to minimise turbo lag caused by the greater “inertia” when a turbocharger with a larger impeller reaches full speed.

This had brought undoubted advantages in terms of responsiveness at the start, when the lights turned green; however, these were effectively negated by the PRE-START phase, which allows the engines to accelerate in neutral for five seconds to build up turbo pressure, thereby eliminating turbo lag.

The elimination of this advantage effectively placed the Ferrari engine at a performance disadvantage at high RPMs on the straights, precisely because of the lower power output resulting from the use of a smaller turbocharger.

It is therefore obvious that, when defining the upgrade to be introduced using the second ADUO, the Maranello engineers focused their attention on adopting a turbocharger with a larger diameter than the previous one.

It is accurate to consider this a significant modification, as the adoption of a larger turbocharger has countless implications for combustion, electronic ignition management, fuel consumption, and the power and torque delivery curves.

In essence, although this mid-season change cannot be strictly classified as structural, it is undeniable that it effectively involved modifying all the power unit’s operating parameters.

This obviously implies substantial repercussions in terms of electrical charge management, a crucial factor for these power units. The availability of greater power under specific operating conditions thus becomes essential to “address”, without completely eliminating, the shortcomings exhibited by the Maranello power unit at the start of the season.

It is correct, in fact, to consider that the Scuderia, by virtue of the regulations governing ADUOs, has two additional evolutionary updates to implement for 2027.

Therefore, the upgrades introduced at Monza, characterised by the new turbo, but also by the analysis and adaptation of all aspects related to combustion, the other part of the internal combustion engine represent the foundation upon which the 2027 upgrades will be built, with the first of these effectively constituting the base version of next year’s power unit.

Going into as much numerical detail as possible regarding the performance increase of the current PU, rumours suggest that bench test data showed an increase of over 2% in the power produced by the internal combustion engine, thanks in part to refinements made to the Shell fuel, which were carried out in parallel with the development of the power unit.

In short, the heart of the SF-26 seems to be beating stronger than ever.

title: Lewis Hamilton delivers clear verdict on latest Ferrari boost
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has stated Ferrari's engine upgrade at Monza will not completely allow it to overcome the deficit to its rivals.

Ferrari has been known to lack pace in a straight line throughout the opening half of the 2026 season.

The Maranello-based squad brought its first engine upgrade to Austria earlier this year and then targeted its home event at the Italian Grand Prix for a second modification.

It has struggled for form at the last two rounds and has failed to clinch a podium in that period - but Hamilton is keen to end that streak and seal his first win as a Ferrari driver on the team's soil.

Having already won twice this year, Ferrari is pushing to keep the pressure on championship leaders Mercedes, leaving Hamilton proud of the effort.

“Every little helps,” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“Up until this point of the year, we’ve been losing, even in the last race on such a short circuit, we were losing four tenths a lap through the race.

“So that’s a huge deficit and we’ve carried that through the year to this point.

“And what I can say is I’m just really, really proud of when I go back to the factory and I see how hard everyone is working, that they’re really just heads down.

“Everyone’s so enthusiastic. I see a different focus this year to last year. Last year, I felt like there wasn’t really a North Star.

“We were kind of, I think, doing the best we could, but not really knowing where exactly we’re trying to aim for. And now we have a North Star. We know we need to work towards.”

With another engine upgrade set to be deployed on Friday, Hamilton is hopeful it will aid its effort to contend for victory.

However, the seven-time champion admitted the new adjustments will not be enough to draw level with the benchmark.

“I think they’ve done a tremendous job to really pull together and deliver,” he said.

“And this is a step forward. It’s not the whole gap that we need, but we knew that would be the case.

“But to see bits coming each weekend, adding to the car, it’s exciting to see that we are pushing and, you know, strongly still believe that we’ve got what it takes to win.”

title: George Russell plots 'team to beat' target in bold Monza prediction
excerpt:
George Russell believes there could be a four-way battle for victory at the Italian Grand Prix and refused to accept Mercedes as favourites for the weekend at Monza.

The seven-time grand prix winner also feels that the Brackley-based squad can return to the top of the pecking order in the coming rounds.

The W17 has been the benchmark chassis for much of the F1 season, but Lando Norris and McLaren have seized the initiative with back-to-back victories in Hungary and Zandvoort.

Russell, who scored a sprint win and a third-place finish in the Netherlands, is under no illusions about where the competitive picture currently stands.

"When you look at the past couple of races and how competitive Lando and McLaren have been, it's definitely very fair to say that they are the team to beat right now," Russell told media, including RacingNews365.

The British driver conceded that Mercedes is currently an upgrade behind its rivals, but expressed confidence in the team's underlying chassis performance, with the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia thought to be the likely point at which the team introduces further developments.

"We know we're an upgrade behind most, and we hope we can go back to being the team to beat in a couple of races' time," he said. "But for now, the fight is with McLaren. Ferrari has got the upgrades this weekend..."

A four-team race at Monza

The Scuderia will roll out a significant development package at Monza, including a revised floor, an updated version of its 'Macarena' rear wing, a new front wing and the second ADUO power-unit specification, which is estimated to deliver around 15 horsepower.

Despite the challenge from McLaren and Ferrari, Russell drew attention to his own team's strong weekend at Zandvoort, where Mercedes took a double podium in the race alongside his sprint victory.

"I actually think we came away from Zandvoort having a very positive weekend as a team, and I think a P2 and a P3 and a sprint win was actually probably better than the car's true performance," he added.

Red Bull, too, is expected to thrive at the power-sensitive Temple of Speed, with the RB22's strong power unit and low-drag efficiency well suited to Monza's long straights. Russell acknowledged as much, while stopping short of naming any single team as the outright favourite.

"I don't know if we can say we're favourites this weekend, but we definitely probably have a greater opportunity than we've had in the last two races, where it's been less about the power unit and more about the chassis," he said.

"And, as I said, I think we definitely have had the best chassis, and I think we'll do again in the upcoming races.

"We can't forget Red Bull has a very strong power unit as well. We know this circuit is going to suit them more than the others.

"Ferrari [is] with the upgrade, so I think it can be a four-team race this weekend. It's so close right now that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference between a couple of positions, which can change the podium. So yeah, right now I don't know who is going to be the team to beat."

title: Oscar Piastri explains 'chaos' theory as F1 faces 'pretty extraordinary' Italian GP
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has predicted a potentially "chaotic" and "pretty extraordinary" Italian Grand Prix, with Formula 1's new-for-2026 energy management challenges set to come sharply back into focus at Monza.

As is well-trodden ground, the revised power unit regulations have made energy recovery and deployment a defining consideration this year.

With the MGU-H removed and the electrical contribution of the hybrid system significantly increased, teams are far more reliant on recovering sufficient energy through braking, partial throttle, lift-off regeneration and super clipping.

That creates particular problems at energy-starved circuits, where cars spend long periods at full throttle but have relatively limited opportunities to harvest energy.

Like Silverstone, Monza is an extreme example of this. The difficulty is a fundamental one: giving teams more energy to recover encourages excessive harvesting and super clipping, while reducing the allowance limits the energy available to deploy on the straights, thus hindering top speeds.

The FIA moved to address that balance with a mid-season revision to the regulations, reducing the standard qualifying recharge threshold and expanding the number of events at which alternative limits can be used. The changes were aimed at reducing excessive harvesting and making qualifying more consistently flat-out, with the FIA targeting significantly shorter periods of super clipping.

Monza will be at the extreme end of that scale, with a 5MJ qualifying limit and 7MJ in the race. The 5MJ figure is the lowest qualifying allowance currently forecast for any circuit, reflecting just how difficult it is to replenish the battery around the Temple of Speed.

Piastri believes the governing body's intervention has chosen the preferable of two difficult options, even if the revised regulations will continue to create complications.

"You just don't really have much energy to use," the McLaren driver told media, including RacingNews365. "At a circuit like this, you've got a problem no matter which direction you go.

"If the harvest limit was higher, we would be super clipping everywhere and probably losing 30 or 40 kph at the end of each straight.

"But they've dropped the harvest limit, which means super clipping is a normal-ish amount or, let's say, a reasonable amount.

"It's still there, but also you then don't have as much energy to spend on the straights, so the actual top speed is quite low. So we'll wait and see what top speeds we get.

"In our sim running, I think we were actually quicker on the front straight in Hungary than we were here, which, yeah, doesn't make a whole lot of sense, but it's more that we just don't have the energy to spend.

"But again, if you gave us the energy to spend, we then don't have anywhere to harvest it. So you run into a problem no matter which way you go. And for me, I think this is the correct direction to go in and have a sensible amount of super clipping."

Why the Italian Grand Prix could be 'pretty extraordinary'

The consequences could be particularly significant in the grand prix itself. The new regulations give teams and drivers more strategic choices over when electrical energy is deployed, while the Overtake Mode can also alter how long a pursuing car can sustain its performance advantage.

That could produce unusual differences in straight-line performance and overtaking opportunities, particularly as drivers begin the race with varying energy strategies.

While Piastri was less certain over the impact on one-lap pace, he expects the opening stages of Sunday's race to provide a striking demonstration of the challenges facing F1's new generation of machinery.

"Qualifying, I'm not sure how much it will impact things," the nine-time grand prix winner added. "We'll find out probably a bit more through Friday.

"I think the race is going to be chaos, especially at the beginning. It's obviously a track that's very, very energy-starved and a lot of different straights where you can use your energy. So the racing could be pretty extraordinary.

"Let's see what we get. We've got a lot of track time until then, so we'll see what kind of deployment everybody has, and where it all pans out.

"But I'm expecting it to be pretty chaotic, [or] exciting. Pick or choose which perspective you want on that, but it's going to be eventful one way or another."

title: Max Verstappen addresses potential Liam Lawson help: 'I never ask'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen does not expect Red Bull to use Liam Lawson to help his qualifying efforts at the Italian Grand Prix, with slipstreaming expected to be prevalent at Monza.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion insists he does not make such requests to the Milton Keynes-based team, and does not plan on doing so this weekend, despite the New Zealander being a stand-in for his regular team-mate Isack Hadjar, who is still suffering the effects of the wrist injury that ruled him out of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Slipstreaming, which is essentially having the driver in front punch a hole in the air for you, is still an effective tool to be used, but is far less widespread in contemporary F1 than in eras gone by, with the advantage of sacrificing clean air for a tow no longer as advantageous as it once was.

That means teams rarely deploy one driver strategically in qualifying to aid the other. However, the visit to the Temple of Speed is often a departure from the norm, and this season is expected to be no different.

In fact, the effect is expected to be amplified at Monza under the new F1 regulations. The FIA has set the harvesting limit at a low 5 MJ in qualifying — and 7 MJ in the race — on the energy-starved circuit, and the impact is expected to be extreme.

This is due to the subsequent low top speeds and the benefit it will also have on energy use, with those following a car ahead closely having to use less battery deployment in relative terms, which can then be used elsewhere throughout the lap.

When questioned about whether he anticipates following within a second, or even half a second, will be common practice in qualifying, Verstappen expressed his lack of interest in playing strategic games on his push laps.

"Not sure within a second, [but] maybe a bit closer than what you have seen in the last few years," the Dutchman told media, including RacingNews365.

"It's also so easy to put yourself in a s****y place on track. We've seen it a few years ago, when it was a big mess.

"Honestly, I just think with what we are doing at the moment, I'm not really looking for that; I just want to do my laps and try and get the car in a good window."

And the 28-year-old has no intention of having Lawson's focus be helping him achieve his lap times when the fight for pole reaches Q3.

"Honestly, no, I haven't really thought about that," the 71-time grand prix winner said.

"If you're fighting in a championship battle, or you really try and do something special... but they [the team] want two cars trying to do well, but let's see.

"I never ask things to the team, and I leave it up to them for these kinds of things. I think that's best."

title: F1 teams agree plan to reduce 2027 grand prix distances - report
excerpt:
All 11 F1 teams have reached an agreement to reduce the distance of grands prix from the usual 305km to 290km for the 2027 season. Here is why...

F1 grands prix are set to become shorter for the 2027 Formula 1 season, with teams having unanimously backed a proposal to reduce the standard race distance from 305km to approximately 290km, according to multiple reports.

The move would see most races trimmed by roughly two to three laps. Monaco, which already runs to a reduced distance of 260km, would be unaffected by the change.

The push to shorten races stems from a knock-on effect of technical adjustments being made to the 2027 regulations.

Following tweaks to power unit rules at a relatively late stage, fuel-flow rates are being increased for next season to prevent cars from becoming too energy-starved during races.

However, pushing more fuel through the engine also means more fuel is required to complete a full race distance.

That created a headache for teams that had already sized their fuel tanks around the original 2026 power unit specifications and had no desire to build an entirely new car for 2027.

Some additional cost cap allowance has been made available to teams planning to carry over their chassis, giving them extra financial headroom to make the necessary modifications. Reducing race distances was identified as a further way of easing the burden.

What happens now?

Initial discussions centred on cutting a handful of specific races by a couple of laps rather than applying a blanket reduction across the calendar. A further adjustment was also proposed in the form of limiting drivers to a single formation lap prior to the start, rather than multiple warming laps.

As talks progressed, however, it became apparent that having varying race distances throughout the season could create unintended consequences. It is understood that certain events risked turning into fuel-economy runs rather than genuine wheel-to-wheel contests, which was clearly not the intended outcome.

Following dialogue between the FIA and the teams, it was agreed that a single, consistent grand prix distance for the entire season would be preferable, mirroring the approach already in place. That proposal has since received unanimous backing from all teams on the grid.

Before the shorter distances can be written into the 2027 sporting regulations, the proposal must first be formally approved by the F1 Commission, which comprises the teams, the FIA and the Formula 1 Management (FOM). It will subsequently require ratification by the FIA's World Motor Sport Council.

It is understood that the reduction is currently agreed only for 2027, given that it arose as a direct consequence of the late-stage power unit rule changes.

Whether it becomes a permanent fixture beyond that season may depend on how further fuel-flow modifications planned for 2028 interact with the technical package of the cars competing at that time.

title: Liam Lawson reveals 'quite late' Red Bull call as Isack Hadjar pain persists
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has another chance to show Red Bull just what he can do in Monza.

Liam Lawson has revealed he was told by Red Bull on Wednesday that he would again replace Isack Hadjar, a decision he admitted came "quite late".

Hadjar remains on the sidelines for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix due to persistent wrist pain following an injury sustained while training during the summer break.

As at Zandvoort a fortnight ago, Lawson has been called up from Racing Bulls to replace the Frenchman, while Yuki Tsunoda is again alongside Arvid Lindblad in the sister outfit.

Lawson knew there was a strong chance he would be back in the RB22 at Monza, and he still managed to complete his usual pre-race prep despite the late decision for Hadjar to sit out.

Asked when he was told he would replace Hadjar again, Lawson told select media, including RacingNews365: "Wednesday. So, for the last week, it's been sort of just waiting to see.

"Obviously, trying to give Isack the best chance as well for his recovery. But, yeah, I think in the back of my mind, I knew that obviously there was still a chance.

"But, obviously, only being on Wednesday, it felt quite late, but we had enough time to still do a simulator session and normal prep for the weekend."

Lawson's second chance

Monza represents another chance for Lawson to show Red Bull just what he can do, particularly after impressing in Zandvoort.

Despite only having one practice session due to it being a Sprint event, Lawson went on to make Q3 and finish the Dutch GP in seventh.

By having the traditional format in Monza, Lawson is expecting a less stressful event and more time to settle into the RB22.

Discussing what his mindset is going into the weekend, Lawson replied: "Just try and make the most of it. Again, I think, yeah, obviously, it's an interesting position for me to be in.

"And Zandvoort was, yeah, I mean, being a Sprint weekend is obviously quite stressful at times, but overall it was a good weekend.

"And at least now I've had that, you know, it should be a bit easier to adjust. We also have three practice sessions here. It's a much more normal weekend. So, yeah, it's another good opportunity."

title: The F1 rookies taking part in Italian GP FP1
excerpt:
Four rookie drivers will get behind the wheel of an F1 car at Monza this Friday, as teams continue to fulfil their mandatory obligations for the 2026 season.

Under current regulations, each team must run a rookie driver, defined as someone with no more than two grand prix starts, in FP1 on four occasions per season, twice per car.

With the Italian Grand Prix approaching, four teams have opted to use the Monza weekend to tick off part of that requirement.

Ayumu Iwasa will step into Max Verstappen's Red Bull RB22. The Japanese driver is no stranger to FP1 duties, having accumulated seven such outings since 2024 with both Red Bull and Racing Bulls.

Luke Browning, a Williams Academy product with six previous FP1 appearances to his name, will replace Alex Albon in the FW48.

Alpine's Paul Aron, who has already racked up eight FP1 sessions split between Audi and Alpine in 2025, takes over Pierre Gasly's A526.

But perhaps the most intriguing name is Colton Herta, the American IndyCar star who will drive Sergio Perez's Cadillac for his third FP1 outing of 2026, having made his debut in the format at Barcelona earlier this season.

title: Lando Norris raises McLaren concern as biggest weakness set for ultimate exposure
excerpt:
Lando Norris has raised concerns that Monza will expose McLaren’s key weakness in chicanes and general low-speed corners at this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix.

Norris enters the event full of confidence, with momentum firmly behind him after securing back-to-back victories either side of the summer break in Hungary and the Netherlands.

This has seen him move to within 83 points of championship leader Kimi Antonelli and left many believing that the defending world champion could yet be a title contender once again.

However, Monza is a circuit that is not expected to be as strong for the Woking-based outfit as the recent rounds, largely due to the style of corners.

McLaren has struggled in chicanes and slow-speed corners since the start of the new power-unit regulations, something of which Monza has several.

It is a legendary venue boasting high-speed straights, followed by heavy braking and tight chicanes, with Norris conceding that the papaya squad does not have an immediate fix.

Asked if McLaren has a fix for its chicane and slow speed corner weakness, Norris told select media, including RacingNews365: "No, there’s not a lot we can do, really.

"It’s just that every car has strengths and weaknesses and is designed in slightly different ways, and ours is just not quite where we want it to be in that style of corner and at that speed. But clearly, we are also able to extract more performance in other types of corners.

"So it’s just the style of F1 that everyone has kind of strengths and weaknesses. It’s obviously something we acknowledge, which is a good thing, and we’re trying to work on it as quickly as possible. Sometimes things can be quick in F1, sometimes not.

"So it’s stuff that the whole team is working on back at the factory, and it’s more just that there’s clear acknowledgement that this has been our biggest weakness lately, and we know that we might struggle again here in those styles of corners."

Compromising high-speed performance

McLaren’s real hope of being strong in the slow-speed corners this weekend would be to compromise its top speed.

It is a decision Norris and the team will have to make, although the Briton has recognised that it is not a change which will guarantee an improvement.

"So we’ll see what we can do to maybe compromise a little bit on the high speed to try and get something in the slow speed," added Norris.

"But if it were simple, we would do a lot more of it. So it’s not as simple as simply doing that at the same time. So, yeah, we’ll see. We know it’s a place we have to work on."

title: Charles Leclerc confirms Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 'priority' at Italian GP
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has stated that Lewis Hamilton has “priority” over where to place his car in the queue this weekend at the Italian Grand Prix.

The Monza F1 track contains several long straights, making it one of the fastest tracks on the schedule.

Slipstreaming has been an important factor in extracting lap time around the venue, but it is set to be even more prominent this weekend due to the new-for-2026 power units, which will likely see the cars lose speed at the end of straights as the battery depletes.

In qualifying, cars will be chasing any slipstream they can to punch a hole in the air and reduce drag - and for Hamilton, he may find it easier than his team-mate.

“For the slipstream, we've always had the same philosophy over the years, where one time Lewis has the priority to choose where he wants to start, and one weekend it's on me,” Leclerc told media including RacingNews365.

“This weekend, Lewis will have the priority, so I guess we'll go for a slipstream.

“Whether we are going to compromise one qualifying [for] the other, I don't think that will happen.

“If we can help each other, trying to start the lap at the optimum distance between each other, that will be done.

“I'll try to find another slipstream off someone else, hoping to put myself in the best possible place.”

On Sunday, it is anticipated that there will be a return of 'yo-yo racing', which was a common feature during the early season grands prix.

When asked if it will be equally as important to work with his team-mate during the race as it is in qualifying, Leclerc said: ”For the race, that is a very valid point.

“We've started to look at it now for quite a few days and trying to understand.

“It's also very, very difficult to predict because the thing is that once you are in the car, it always looks nice from outside.

“But the difference is sometimes that much that it is very difficult to react to the car in front.

“It's not that you can avoid yo-yo racing if you end up in a situation like this, but we'll try to do the best possible job and try to do better.”
